newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr sidelined by US$, choppy on yen.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr sidelined by US$, choppy on yen.

text.p: The Australian dollar spent Tuesday sidelined against its U.S. counterpart but went on another raucous ride on the yen which saw it career as far as the 91.00 level as Japanese buyers piled in.

It stumbled later as Japanese offcials made conflicting comments on the wisdom of the yen's fall and Australian ministers talked up the chances of a domestic rate cut. But still ended firm on the day and dealers looked for further gains as Japanese investors fled record low rates at home.
Life with the U.S. dollar was much more pedestrian, with few seeing any chance of escaping a US$0.7880/7950 range near term.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar was idling at US$0.7910/15 having wandered aimlessly between US$0.7928 to US$0.7905 through the day. That was not far distant from Monday's US$0.7925/30.
It kept some gains on the yen to end at 90.45/55 from 90.20/30 Monday, but could not sustain the early peak of 91.05.

That foray atop 91.00, its first since September 1994, came after a tide of buying out of Tokyo linked to dual currency samurai bond issues and from offshore investors looking to borrow cheaply in yen and lend for fat profits in dollars.
Traders reckoned at least two samurais went through, on top of Monday's 30 billion yen issue and A$350 million of Eurbonds.

The U.S. currency itself stormed past a 42-month old barrier at 113.60 yen Monday and continued on to reach 114.91 today encouraged by comments from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin that he was not concerned by the dollar's recent rise.

The market had been worried the administration would call for a lower dollar to boost U.S. exports and improve the country's trade deficit. But Rubin said he favoured a strong dollar as it reduced inflation and lowered interest rates.
Dollar bulls did pause, however, when Japan's influential Trade Ministry said the yen had fallen to levels where stabilisation would be favourable.
The situation was further confused when Finance Minister Wataru Kubo said current forex moves were not a big problem, suggesting the authorities were not of one mind on the yen.
Dealers decided to take profits just in case and the U.S. dollar retreated to 114.33/38, dragging the Aussie with it.

Looking past the confusion, traders saw plenty of reason for investors to keep switching out of yen given Japan's sluggish economy meant rates there were likely to remain at record lows for months to come. The yield on Japan's 10 year bond, for instance, fell to a 10-month low of 2.595 percent today, while the comparable Australian bond offered 7.48 percent.
However, the market strongly suspects official rates will be cut here before year-end and the narrowing in the dollar's premium, particularly on the US$, may discourage Japanese funds.

Both Treasurer Peter Costello and Prime Minister John Howard were out talking up the prospects for a cut and most analysts continued to expect an easing after the Reserve Bank's board meeting next Tuesday.

The first of the week's domestic data are out Wednesday but given the market's preoccupation with monetary policy the September current account deficit is unlikely to cause a ripple unless well outside median forecasts of A$1.3 billion.
This would be the fourth sub-A$1.5 billion result in a row and compares with average monthly deficits in 1995/96 of A$1.66 billion.
Dealers said such a result would be supportive for the dollar at the margin, but the market has become used to the improved trend and usually reacts with a yawn.

A deficit outcome in line with forecasts would, however, suggest net exports will make a healthy contribution to third quarter GDP growth of between 0.6 and 1.0 percent compared to a detraction of 0.9 percent in Q2.
